notes.bp: Listeners must infer whether a speaker means the opposite of the words, even when the words themselves sound positive.
notes.wh: Irony depends on timing and pitch accents as well as lexical content, and listeners from different varieties may use those cues differently.
notes.naive: Treat the words or one global pitch statistic as sufficient for sarcasm.
notes.ap: Vary prenuclear and nuclear accent placement/type and measure regional listeners' sarcasm decisions and response times.
notes.mech: German utterances are presented in seven prosodic conditions to listeners from Freiburg and Trier, who classify them as sarcastic or sincere.
notes.math: The experiment separates cue presence, accent type, region, decision, and reaction time rather than reducing intonation to one pitch average.
notes.ww: Prenuclear accent presence and especially L*+H nuclear accents drive irony judgments; some conditions also yield faster ironic responses.
notes.limits: The utterances, regions, prosodic manipulations, and binary judgment task bound the result; other languages and natural conversations remain open.
notes.title: Are You Being Sarcastic? Prosodic Cues to Irony Perception in German

notes.bp: A speech recognizer should serve Sardinian varieties despite fragmented data and internal linguistic diversity.
notes.wh: Low-resource languages lack enough transcribed, balanced, and variety-labeled speech for ordinary training recipes.
notes.naive: Pool whatever recordings exist and report one aggregate score that hides variety differences.
notes.ap: Build a reproducible audio-text corpus with explicit variety annotation and evaluate both pretrained and fine-tuned recognizers across varieties.
notes.mech: SardinianVoxes contains about 170 hours of transcribed speech, and the paper defines a benchmark for state-of-the-art and fine-tuned speech-to-text models.
notes.math: A corpus is a measurement object: coverage, transcription, variety labels, and split design determine what an error rate means.
notes.ww: The paper contributes a public resource and evaluation protocol intended to make Sardinian speech technology measurable.
notes.limits: The reported resource, varieties, transcription quality, and benchmark models bound the claim; future collection and independent use are still needed.
notes.title: SardinianVoxes: A Speech Recognition Dataset for the Sardinian Languages

notes.bp: Enhancement should make dysarthric speech easier to understand or recognize without changing the speaker into an artificial typical voice.
notes.wh: Dysarthric speech varies greatly and enhancement can improve a recognizer while damaging intelligibility or perceived quality.
notes.naive: Optimize a generic noise-reduction score and assume lower noise means better recognition.
notes.ap: Compare two diffusion enhancers with a signal-processing baseline on typical and dysarthric speech, then measure ASR, objective quality, and listener judgments.
notes.mech: The systems enhance two English dysarthric corpora; Whisper-Turbo is evaluated before and after enhancement and fine-tuning.
notes.math: The paper treats intelligibility, speech quality, and recognition as separate targets, exposing disagreement between them.
notes.ww: The study reports a systematic comparison rather than a single score; gains and tradeoffs depend on corpus, enhancer, and evaluation target.
notes.limits: The corpora, listener tests, Whisper model, and enhancement settings bound the result; a recognition gain is not automatically a clinical benefit.
notes.title: Objective and Subjective Evaluation of Diffusion-Based Speech  Enhancement for Dysarthric Speech

notes.bp: A detector should say where a fake voice came from, not only that it sounds fake.
notes.wh: Open-set generators and new vocoders create sources not seen during training, and a binary label cannot explain origin.
notes.naive: Train a binary real/fake classifier and treat its confidence as source identity.
notes.ap: Define few-shot identification and verification protocols that trace a generator or one of its components under open-set conditions.
notes.mech: Models are trained on internal and MLAAD data and evaluated across three ASVspoof sets, MLAAD, and Blizzard23.
notes.math: Identification asks which source class matches a few references; verification asks whether a claimed source is supported, making the decision object explicit.
notes.ww: The paper reports discrimination of unseen source attributes and argues for a standardized source-tracing ontology.
notes.limits: Datasets, source taxonomy, reference count, and generator families bound the result; real-world provenance and adversarial adaptation remain open.
notes.title: Audio Deepfake Source Tracing using Multi-Attribute Open-Set Identification and Verification

notes.bp: Emotion recognition should reflect ambiguous human judgments in natural recordings rather than force every clip into one certain label.
notes.wh: Emotions are subjective, classes are imbalanced, and speech and language cues interact.
notes.naive: Train one classifier on hard one-hot labels and sample classes uniformly only after training.
notes.ap: Use cross-modal representation fusion, soft human annotation targets, balanced sampling, multitask learning, and a meta-classifier in stages.
notes.mech: MEDUSA builds an ensemble from self-supervised acoustic and linguistic representations, uses Manifold MixUp, and combines predictions with a trainable meta-classifier.
notes.math: Soft targets preserve disagreement; balanced sampling changes which examples influence learning; the meta-classifier learns when component predictions should be trusted.
notes.ww: MEDUSA ranked first in the naturalistic categorical emotion challenge task reported by the paper.
notes.limits: Challenge splits, annotation distributions, modalities, and ranking define the result; a leaderboard position does not establish emotion truth or cross-cultural validity.
notes.title: Medusa: A Multimodal Deep Fusion Multi-Stage Training Framework for Speech Emotion Recognition in Naturalistic Conditions

notes.bp: A listener or robot should locate several overlapping sounds in three dimensions even when noise and reverberation distort the binaural cues.
notes.wh: Sources can overlap, source count may be unknown, and reflections blur the timing and level differences that encode direction.
notes.naive: Estimate one direction with a fixed-resolution classifier or assume the number of sources in advance.
notes.ap: Use a gated coarse-to-fine model that first detects sectors and then regresses azimuth/elevation with a masked multitask loss.
notes.mech: AuralNet processes binaural signals with multi-head attention, jointly detects sources and estimates azimuth/elevation, and is tested in noisy-reverberant conditions.
notes.math: Classification chooses a spatial sector while regression refines its coordinates; masking lets the loss ignore nonexistent sources.
notes.ww: The paper reports superiority over recent methods in its noisy-reverberant multi-source experiments.
notes.limits: The room simulation/recordings, binaural setup, sector design, and source overlap define the claim; far-field microphone arrays and speech-specific attribution remain open.
notes.title: AuralNet: Hierarchical Attention-based 3D Binaural Localization of Overlapping Speakers

notes.bp: A text-to-speech system should reach good quality without spending excessive computation learning every intermediate diffusion state.
notes.wh: Diffusion models learn a long sequence of noisy-to-clean transformations, and the text and speech views contain different information about the target.
notes.naive: Train the diffusion model longer or add more capacity without teaching it what text and speech already agree on.
notes.ap: Align hidden states using both text-guided and speech-guided objectives so the diffusion process starts with more useful semantic structure.
notes.mech: A-DMA aligns contextual text representations and discriminative speech features during diffusion TTS training, then compares convergence and synthesis quality with baselines.
notes.math: Alignment reduces the mismatch between two representations before the generative process; convergence speed and output quality are separate objectives.
notes.ww: The paper reports doubled convergence speed with better performance than its baselines.
notes.limits: The text/speech encoders, datasets, diffusion schedule, and quality measures bound the claim; hardware cost and new languages remain open.
notes.title: Accelerating Diffusion-based Text-to-Speech Model Trainingwith Dual Modality Alignment

notes.bp: An ASR system should understand dysarthric speech even when speakers talk slowly and differ greatly from one another.
notes.wh: Recognizer errors may come from rhythm and voice characteristics rather than word content, but changing them can erase identity or introduce artifacts.
notes.naive: Fine-tune an ASR model directly on scarce dysarthric data and hope it learns a stable pronunciation mapping.
notes.ap: Convert dysarthric speech toward a healthier rhythm and voice using unsupervised rhythm/voice conversion, then test whether ASR benefits.
notes.mech: A syllable-based rhythm model extends RnV conversion; LF-MMI and Whisper are trained or fine-tuned with converted speech and tested on Torgo.
notes.math: The intervention separates a conversion target from the recognition target; WER reveals whether the transformed signal is easier for ASR.
notes.ww: The paper reports significant LF-MMI WER reductions, especially for more severe dysarthria, while Whisper fine-tuning changes little.
notes.limits: Torgo, conversion artifacts, severity labels, ASR architectures, and WER bound the result; intelligibility, speaker identity, and clinical acceptability need separate tests.
notes.title: Unsupervised Rhythm and Voice Conversion to Improve ASR on Dysarthric Speech
